package.title: Keep Your Muscle on a GLP-1: What the Trials Show + a Simple Plan

social.instagram_caption:
Will you lose muscle on a GLP-1? Here's what the trials actually show 💪

Swipe through:
→ In STEP 1, semaglutide users lost 14.9% of body weight at 68 weeks vs 2.4% on placebo
→ In SURMOUNT-1, people on the highest tirzepatide dose lost 20.9% at 72 weeks vs 3.1% on placebo (separate trials, not a head-to-head)
→ Across GLP-1-based drug trials (36–72 weeks) that used body scans, lean mass made up 25–39% of the weight lost (Neeland et al., 2024). Lean mass includes water and organs, not just muscle, and some lean loss happens with any weight loss, whether from dieting, surgery or medicine
→ In STEP 1's body-scan subgroup (about 140 people), fat mass actually fell more than lean mass — lean mass ended up a bigger share of body weight afterward

The plan that can help: protein at meals (start your plate with it) + strength training 2+ days a week + the WHO's 150–300 minutes of moderate cardio (or 75–150 vigorous) a week.

Have kidney disease? Ask your care team about your protein target first. And ask your prescriber whether a GLP-1 is right for you.

Save this for your next grocery run 🛒 and send it to your gym buddy.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation.

social.facebook_caption:
If you're on (or considering) a GLP-1 medicine, you've probably wondered: am I going to lose muscle along with the fat?

Here's the honest answer from the research. In STEP 1, people on semaglutide lost 14.9% of body weight over 68 weeks (vs. 2.4% on placebo). In SURMOUNT-1, people on the highest tirzepatide dose lost 20.9% over 72 weeks (vs. 3.1% on placebo) — these are separate trials, not a head-to-head comparison. Across GLP-1-based drug trials (36–72 weeks) that used body scans, lean mass — which includes water and organs, not just muscle — made up 25–39% of the weight lost. Some lean loss happens with weight loss from dieting and surgery too, not just GLP-1s. And in STEP 1's body-scan subgroup (about 140 people), fat mass actually fell more than lean mass.

The good news: protein at each meal plus strength training (the WHO suggests 2+ days a week) can help your body hold onto muscle. Swipe through for the full framework. Have kidney disease? Ask your care team about your protein target first, and ask your prescriber whether a GLP-1 is right for you.

factcheck.summary: The carousel is accurate, balanced and safe. The main numbers check out: STEP 1 was 14.9% vs 2.4% at 68 weeks. SURMOUNT-1 was 20.9% on the 15 mg dose vs 3.1% on placebo at 72 weeks, and the slide correctly says these weren't compared head-to-head. The STEP 1 body-scan (DXA) subgroup had about 140 people, fat fell more than lean mass and the lean share of body weight went up. The WHO adult activity numbers are right. The 2025 joint advisory does say "Protein-rich foods can be consumed first in a meal." Safety is handled well: there's a kidney-disease caveat on the protein advice, a joint and heart caveat on strength training, creatine is framed as unproven, there's no dosing, and the CTA has the "ask your prescriber" line. Six minor fixes are listed below, all copy-paste ready: 1) The title promises a "5-part" structure the slides don't have. 2) Slide 5 should name the advisory it paraphrases. 3) The claim on slide 4 that dieting and surgery also cause lean loss has no cited source, though s4 (the JAMA Viewpoint) is already in the source list and should be cited. 4) Nothing cites the creatine source, and it doesn't cover GLP-1 users, so the slide wording should stay as hedged as it is. 5) The Cardio "How hard" cell should match the vigorous option in the "How much" row. 6) I couldn't open the full Neeland 2024 abstract (PubMed showed a CAPTCHA and Wiley returned 403). The 25–39% over 36–72 weeks figure is widely credited to this work, but I couldn't read it in the primary text. I verified s1–s3 and s5–s7 against pages I could reach. For s4 I confirmed the citation (JAMA 2024, Conte, Hall, Klein) but couldn't read the text itself.

issues.claim: Keep Your Muscle on a GLP-1: The 5-Part Checklist
issues.problem: The carousel isn't built as a 5-part checklist. The only 5-item list is the questions for your prescriber on slide 7. The practical plan is really protein first plus strength and cardio. So the title promises something the slides don't cleanly deliver.
issues.fix: Keep Your Muscle on a GLP-1: What the Trials Show + a Simple Plan

issues.claim: That's expert nutrition advice for GLP-1 users.
issues.problem: This is correct: the 2025 joint advisory says "Protein-rich foods can be consumed first in a meal to increase the likelihood of sufficient consumption". But the slide doesn't say who the experts are, and s5 isn't linked anywhere on the slides.
issues.fix: When your appetite is small, eat the protein part of your plate first. That's advice from a 2025 joint advisory by four US nutrition and obesity medicine societies. Have kidney disease? Ask your care team for your protein target first.

issues.claim: This isn't unique to GLP-1s. It happens with dieting and surgery too.
issues.problem: This is accurate, but no source is linked to it. s4 (Conte, Hall & Klein, JAMA 2024) is in the source list and covers this point, but no slide cites it.
issues.fix: This isn't unique to GLP-1s. It happens with dieting and surgery too (JAMA Viewpoint, 2024).

issues.claim: 25–39% lean mass share across GLP-1-based trials of 36–72 weeks, per a 2024 review by Neeland et al.
issues.problem: I couldn't open the primary abstract (PubMed CAPTCHA, Wiley 403). Secondary sources consistently credit the ~25–39% over 36–72 weeks figure to Neeland and colleagues (2024), and the paper exists as cited. The wording already says it's a range and that lean mass isn't just muscle, which is the right framing.
issues.fix: No text change needed. Before publishing, check the exact figure against the full text at https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.15728. If it's worded differently there, change it to "About 25–39%".

issues.problem: The 'How much' row already includes the vigorous option (75–150 min), but the 'How hard' cell for Cardio says only moderate, so the two cells don't match.

issues.claim: Should I consider creatine? An early idea, not yet proven on GLP-1s
issues.problem: This is framed properly as unproven. But s7 (ISSN 2017) is about creatine in general and doesn't mention GLP-1 medicines, so it can't back anything GLP-1-specific. The current wording is fine. Just don't make it any stronger in captions.
issues.fix: Keep the current wording. In captions and packaging, don't imply that creatine has been tested alongside GLP-1 medicines.
